title: PAUL SAID SINGLENESS COULD BE A GIFT—Not a Punishment for People Who Couldn’t Find a Spouse
paragraphs: PAUL SAID SINGLENESS COULD BE A GIFT—Not a Punishment for People Who Couldn’t Find a Spouse
What if the season you keep asking God to end is not evidence that He forgot you—but a place where Christ wants to become so precious that your relationship status can no longer determine your worth?
There is a particular kind of silence that can make a single Christian question everything.
It happens after the wedding invitation arrives.
Again.
You smile when you open it. You really are happy for them.
At least you want to be.
But somewhere between seeing their engagement photographs and reading the words “together with their families,” something inside you aches.
You close your phone.
The room suddenly feels quieter than it did five minutes ago.
And then comes the question you are almost ashamed to ask God.
“Lord… what about me?”
Maybe you have prayed.
Maybe your friends have prayed.
Maybe someone at church has told you, “Your person is coming.”
Maybe people keep treating your singleness like a waiting room—as though real adulthood, real family, real usefulness, or real happiness will finally begin when another human being chooses you.
And perhaps that is what hurts most.
Not merely being single.
But feeling as though everyone assumes something is missing from you.
Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that interrupts that entire way of thinking.
Something almost shocking in a culture—including Christian culture—that can quietly make marriage feel like graduation and singleness feel like being held back.
Paul writes:
Hekastos idion echei charisma ek Theou.
In context, the phrase means that each person has his own gift from God.
That word matters.
χάρισμα — charisma.
Gift.
Grace-gift.
Something received from God.
Paul does not look at the unmarried believer and automatically say, “Something went wrong.”
He does not say, “You failed to find somebody.”
He does not say, “God loves married Christians more.”
He does not say, “Once you finally get married, your real life can begin.”
In 1 Corinthians 7:7, while discussing marriage, sexual self-control, and unmarried life, Paul says that each person has a particular gift from God, “one of one kind and one of another.”
Read that again slowly.
Because somebody has spent years calling a punishment what Paul was willing to call a gift.
That does not mean every unmarried Christian necessarily possesses a permanent lifelong calling to celibacy.
Paul's words should not be twisted into telling every lonely single believer, “Stop wanting marriage. This must be your gift.”
The same chapter honors marriage.
Paul recognizes sexual desire.
He acknowledges different circumstances and different callings.
He is not anti-marriage.
He is destroying the idea that marriage is the only spiritually meaningful way to live.
And that changes everything.
Because perhaps your deepest problem is not that you are single.
Perhaps it is that somewhere along the way, you started believing that another human being would finally prove you were worth loving.
That marriage would validate you.
That a ring would silence insecurity.
That being chosen romantically would finally answer the question:
“Am I enough?”
And that is where the Gospel has to go deeper than relationship advice.
Because Jesus Christ did not shed His blood so that your ultimate identity could hang on whether another human being wants to marry you.
Before anyone places a ring on your finger, there was a Savior who allowed nails to be driven through His hands.
Before anybody says, “I choose you,” the Gospel announces something infinitely greater to everyone who belongs to Christ:
You have been redeemed at immeasurable cost.
Your worth is not established by your desirability.
Your identity is not “single.”
Your identity is not “married.”
Your identity is not “divorced.”
Your identity is not “rejected.”
Your identity is not “the one nobody chose.”
If you are in Christ, your life has been claimed by Jesus.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts so deeply.
Because sometimes we do not merely want marriage.
We want marriage to save us from ourselves.
We want somebody to make the loneliness disappear.
Somebody to heal the insecurity.
Somebody to prove the ex was wrong.
Somebody to erase the embarrassment of still being single.
Somebody to make us feel wanted.
But that is an unbearable weight to place upon another human being.
Your future husband cannot be your Messiah.
Your future wife cannot be your Messiah.
Marriage is beautiful, but marriage makes a terrible god.
Only Jesus can carry the weight of being your Savior.
And Paul knew something else we often forget.
Singleness can create something extraordinarily valuable:
availability.

Later in the chapter, Paul explains that an unmarried believer can have a particular freedom to be concerned with “the things of the Lord” and with pleasing the Lord. He then makes his purpose unmistakable: he is not trying to trap believers or put a restraint around their necks. He wants what promotes good order and undivided devotion to the Lord.
The Greek expression in 1 Corinthians 7:35 is striking:
εὐπάρεδρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως
It carries the idea of devoted attendance upon the Lord without distraction.
That is the heartbeat.
Not:
“Single people are holier.”
Not:
“Marriage is spiritually inferior.”
Not:
“If you want a spouse, your faith is weak.”
But:
“What can this season become when Jesus truly receives it?”
Imagine discovering that the years you called “wasted” were years God could use.
Imagine realizing that you do not have to postpone obedience until somebody loves you romantically.
You can serve now.
You can pray now.
You can disciple now.
You can travel for the Gospel now.
You can study Scripture now.
You can sit beside the broken now.
You can feed someone now.
You can evangelize now.
You can build something for the Kingdom now.
You can become deeply rooted in Christ now.
You do not need a wedding photograph before God can use your life.
Some of the tragedy surrounding Christian singleness is not singleness itself.
It is how much life people sacrifice waiting for singleness to end.
Years disappear.
They keep saying:
“When I meet someone…”
“When I get married…”
“When I finally have a family…”
Then I will be happy.
Then I will feel complete.
Then I will really start living.
But what if you are standing inside years you will someday wish you had stewarded differently?

What if you eventually marry—and one day look backward and realize you spent your entire single season grieving the absence of something God had not yet given instead of worshiping Him with what He had already placed in your hands?
There are prayers you can pray today.
People you can love today.
Scripture you can learn today.
Sins you can confront today.
Wounds you can bring before Christ today.
People who need the Gospel today.
A Kingdom that is moving today.
Jesus is worthy today.
And there is another truth we need to say carefully.
Sometimes singleness hurts.
Deeply.
There is no need to romanticize loneliness.
There are nights when having nobody beside you hurts.
There are moments when watching friends build families hurts.
There are birthdays when the unanswered prayer feels louder.
There are holidays when an empty chair feels almost cruel.

There are people reading this who genuinely desire marriage—not because they worship marriage, but because they long to love someone faithfully, build a home, raise children, share ordinary mornings, endure difficult years together, grow old together, and serve Jesus beside someone.
That desire is not shameful.
You do not have to pretend you never feel lonely in order to prove that Christ is enough.
Jesus Himself knew sorrow.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
You can tell God:
“I want marriage.”
You can tell Him:
“I am lonely.”
You can tell Him:
“This hurts.”
You can cry while trusting Him.
You can desire marriage while refusing to worship it.
You can pray for a spouse while refusing to make your life meaningless until one arrives.
You can hold desire in one hand and surrender in the other.
And maybe surrender sounds something like this:
“Jesus, I still desire marriage. But I desire You more.
If marriage comes, let it glorify You.
If I must wait, teach me to glorify You while waiting.
Do not let loneliness drive me into counterfeit intimacy.
Do not let desperation make me accept someone who pulls me away from You.
Do not let comparison make me resent the blessings You have given others.
Do not let rejection convince me that I am rejected by You.
Do not let my relationship status become my identity.
My life belongs to You.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because now the question changes.
It is no longer merely:
“God, when will You send somebody?”
It becomes:
“Jesus, what do You want to do with me now?”
And suddenly singleness is no longer merely an empty space between relationships.
It becomes territory where Christ can reign.
Some of you need that truth because loneliness has already been whispering compromises into your ear.
“Just message them.”
“You know they don't love Jesus, but maybe they'll change.”
“Go back to the relationship God already rescued you from.”
“Everybody else is sleeping together.”
“You've waited long enough.”
“You deserve somebody.”
“Nobody has to know.”
And loneliness can make chains look like companionship.
Please hear this:
Do not trade obedience for temporary affection.
Do not abandon Christ just because somebody made you feel wanted.
There are embraces that can pull you farther from God.
There are relationships that answer loneliness by creating bondage.
There are people you can desperately pray for God to give you whom, in His mercy, He may be protecting you from.
The goal is not merely to find somebody.
The goal is faithfulness to Jesus.
And this is where grace enters the scandal.
Maybe your story has not been clean.
Maybe singleness did not make you more devoted to God.
Maybe it made you desperate.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe you lived with someone.
Maybe pornography became the anesthesia for loneliness.
Maybe you slept with somebody because for a few hours being desired felt better than being alone.
Maybe you stayed in a relationship you knew dishonored Christ.
Maybe you have been hiding sexual sin behind worship songs, Bible verses, and Sunday smiles.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And He is not asking you to clean yourself enough to become worthy of returning.
He is calling you to repent and come home.
The cross is where sinners stop hiding.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
Grace does not rename sin so we can comfortably remain inside it.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of what is killing you.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Turn away from it.
Receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps those three words can mark the moment you decided you were finished pretending.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
If you need prayer, simply write:
Let believers gather around believers.
Let honesty replace performance.
Let the Church become family again.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
This is why messages like this need to travel farther than the people who already agree with them.
Someone on your Facebook friends list is quietly interpreting singleness as rejection.
Someone is considering returning to a relationship that nearly destroyed them.
Someone thinks God has forgotten them.
Someone is smiling publicly while privately wondering why nobody has chosen them.
Not for numbers.
For that person.
Send it privately to somebody who would never admit publicly how lonely they have become.
Because loneliness has a strange way of making us forget on Tuesday what God reminded us of on Sunday.
Come back when the wedding photographs hurt again.
Come back when comparison starts talking.
Come back when temptation starts negotiating.
Come back when you need to remember:
Singleness is not proof that God has abandoned you.
And marriage is not proof that God favors somebody more than you.
Jesus is still Lord in both.
It does not.
It does not.
And never because you should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your support can help this work continue.
Your sharing can help it travel.
Your prayers can help sustain it.

And your participation can help create a community where people are not merely consuming Christian content but being continually pointed back to Jesus Christ, Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and Gospel transformation.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Christ already paid the price we never could.
If you would like to stand with Gospel Warrior through monthly support and go deeper with this community:
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker who is asking questions.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of religious rules.
Let them encounter Jesus.
Because Christianity was never ultimately about finding the perfect spouse.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Marriage is temporary.
Singleness is temporary.
Our present bodies are temporary.
This age is temporary.
But Christ is eternal.
So if God gives you a husband, love him for the glory of Jesus.
If God gives you a wife, love her for the glory of Jesus.
If you are waiting, wait with Jesus.
If you remain single, live fully for Jesus.
If your heart has been broken, bring the pieces to Jesus.
If sexual sin has stained your story, repent and run to Jesus.
If rejection convinced you that you were worthless, look again toward Jesus.
Because the greatest love story of your existence was never supposed to begin when another human being finally chose you.
It began with a holy God pursuing sinners through a bloodstained cross and an empty tomb.
Maybe you thought your life was on pause.
It isn't.
Maybe you thought nobody choosing you meant nobody wanted you.
The cross tells a different story.
Maybe you thought singleness was the embarrassing chapter you needed God to hurry up and finish.
But perhaps Christ is writing something in these pages that you will only understand later.
So stop measuring your life by somebody else's timeline.
Stop calling yourself forgotten.
Stop treating your present life like the hallway outside the room where your “real life” will someday begin.
Open your hands.
Give Jesus the longing.
Give Him the loneliness.
Give Him the sexuality.
Give Him the future wedding you have imagined a thousand times.
Give Him the fear that it may never happen.
Give Him all of it.
And then ask the question that can transform an entire season:
“Lord Jesus… if my life belongs completely to You, what can You do with me now?”
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would never have been remaining single.

Perhaps it would have been spending years waiting for another person to make your life meaningful while Jesus Christ—the One for whom you were created—was standing in the middle of those very years saying:
“Give them to Me.”
You were never waiting to become worthy of a love story.
At Calvary, Love Himself had already entered yours.
